0ce1a90d16e8326d: BERLIN: Germany's economy is set to grow by nearly 1.2 per cent in 2026, helped by stronger exports and government spending in the first half, according to new forecats by the German Economic Institute (IW) seen by Reuters on Sunday.
IW had projected growth of only 0.4 per cent in its previous forecasts published in May.
The economic institutes Ifo, DIW, RWI and IMK have also recently raised their forecasts, following a stronger-than-expected first half of the year.
IW warned that momentum would fade in the second half as high energy prices, weak private investment and job losses weigh on demand.
IW forecast slower growth of nearly one per cent in 2027, saying consumption and investment would each contribute about half of the expansion.
IW said real exports would rise 2.8 per cent this year and imports two per cent, after goods exports rose sharply in the second quarter, partly because of inventory effects.
It cautioned that the boost in exports was likely temporary and structural pressures, including high production costs, protectionism and Chinese competition, remained.
Private consumption is expected to increase only 0.3 per cent in 2026, as inflation of more than 2.5 per cent erodes purchasing power.
720b2e63bea2a100: KUALA LUMPUR: Former prime minister Datuk Seri Najib Razak has thanked His Majesty Sultan Ibrahim, the Yang di-Pertuan Agong, for granting him a conditional pardon to serve the remainder of his sentence under house arrest.
The pardon relates to his conviction in the SRC International case.
In a statement issued through his lawyers, Messrs Shafee & Co, Najib also expressed his gratitude to the Federal Territories Pardons Board.

"Our client records his highest gratitude to His Majesty Seri Paduka Baginda Yang di-Pertuan Agong Sultan Ibrahim Ibni Almarhum Sultan Iskandar for graciously exercising the royal prerogative of mercy in his favour, by consenting to a conditional pardon under which he is to serve the remainder of his sentence under house arrest," the lawyers said.
"Our client receives His Majesty's decision with the utmost humility."
The decision allows Najib to serve the remainder of his sentence under house arrest until Aug 23, 2028, subject to payment of RM50 million and other conditions.

Najib remains in Kajang Prison pending fulfilment of the conditions. His lawyers said a significant portion of his assets, bank accounts and properties remained subject to freezing orders and enforcement proceedings.
They said Najib was taking advice and considering his options for meeting the condition.
The Pardons Board comprises the King as chairman, the Attorney-General, the minister responsible for Federal Territories and three other members appointed by the King.
Najib previously received a royal pardon in January 2024, during the tenure of the 16th Yang di-Pertuan Agong, Al-Sultan Abdullah Ri'ayatuddin Al-Mustafa Billah Shah.

At its 61st meeting on Jan 29, 2024, the Federal Territories Pardons Board reduced Najib's 12-year prison sentence by half to six years and his RM210 million fine to RM50 million, bringing forward his scheduled release date to Aug 23, 2028.
Najib began serving his sentence at Kajang Prison on Aug 23, 2022, after the Federal Court upheld his conviction and 12-year jail term in the SRC International case.

f4286d58d3a33dac: NAGOYA: Sprinter Azeem Fahmi is determined to "continue where he left off" when he takes to the track at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games this week.
Azeem was still a teenager when he claimed a surprise bronze medal in the 100m at the Hangzhou Games in 2023.
Now 22, he has made it clear he will not be content with simply making up the numbers at the Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium.
"I'm not going to the Asian Games this time with the mentality of just wanting to do my best," Azeem said recently.
"I'm going with the mentality of wanting to pick up where I left off.
"A lot of people know that I won an unexpected bronze in 2023.
"This time, the goal is to qualify for the final first. That is my first challenge.
"If I get there, I'm confident I can achieve the same thing (bronze) or even better."
Azeem believes his athletics journey is still in its early stages.
He is also aware of the tough opposition awaiting him in Nagoya.
"At the Asian level, there are many more sprinters who are more senior, more experienced and have achieved more than I have," he added.
"I consider myself a young sprinter. I'm still only 22 and have a long way to go."
The men's and women's 100m events begin with the heats on Thursday.

3e1f7ec310ce56b2: KOTA TINGGI: The conditional pardon granted to former prime minister Datuk Seri Najib Razak may displease certain quarters, particularly non-Umno parties, but the Yang di-Pertuan Agong's royal prerogative under the Federal Constitution must not be questioned.
Umno vice-president Datuk Seri Mohamed Khaled Nordin said granting pardons is not unprecedented in the nation's legal landscape.
"Pardons have been granted in numerous cases, whether involving individuals sentenced to death or life imprisonment, and those decisions were accepted without dispute," he said.

"We hope all citizens accept that the power exists and is permissible under the law. It is the absolute prerogative of the Yang di-Pertuan Agong and should not be questioned by any party," he told reporters after attending the Kota Tinggi Parliamentary Maulidur Rasul celebration at Dewan Besar Felda Air Tawar 2 here today.
Khaled, who is also Kota Tinggi member of parliament, added that the decision should not be linked to ongoing efforts aimed at unifying Malay political parties.

"Elections are a separate matter focused on Malay unity, as the community feels that despite having many Malay political parties, its political influence is weakening. This has nothing to do with Najib's pardon," he said.

"Whether Najib is released or not is a separate issue. Malay unity is about safeguarding the community's interests and political standing. If opponents use the pardon issue to influence voters, it is simply political maneuvering," he added.
Commenting on the Tabung Solidariti Najib Razak launched by Umno, he said the party merely intends to render support within its means.
"It shows our sympathy because RM50 million is a substantial sum. While we may not reach that target, the fund reflects what we can do to help," he said.

Last Friday, His Majesty Sultan Ibrahim, King of Malaysia, granted a conditional pardon allowing Najib to serve the remainder of his prison sentence under house arrest until Aug 23, 2028, provided he pays a RM50 million fine.
Umno subsequently launched the solidarity fund to collect public donations, which reportedly raised RM1 million as of 9.30am yesterday.
88ea586a4eeea70b: KUALA LUMPUR: A mobile police station will be set up near former prime minister Najib Razak’s residence at Langgak Duta here from tomorrow to facilitate security arrangements during any transfer from prison to the home.
Sentul police chief Anuar Bakri Salam said the mobile police station is not intended to provide 24-hour security for Najib.
"It is to provide security during his return, including for local and foreign media and neighbours, as well as to prevent traffic congestion, and manage the presence of supporters,” he said.
Asked whether the residence had been designated as the location for Najib’s house arrest, Anuar said police had yet to receive any official confirmation.

“I cannot confirm this because I have not received any information either, but one of Najib’s official residences is under my jurisdiction. There is also a possibility that other residences belonging to him are being considered,” he said.
He said that based on the information he had received, the prisons department would be responsible for monitoring Najib if he serves the remainder of his sentence under house arrest.
He said four prisons department officers had visited the residence yesterday to conduct an inspection and assessment.
“The police will only facilitate Najib’s movement and, at the same time, ensure the safety of the media,” he said.
He said the police deployment during the process is expected to comprise one supervisor and two personnel, supported by a mobile patrol vehicle unit.

Attorney-General Dusuki Mokhtar was yesterday reported as saying the standard operating procedures for Najib’s house arrest would cover matters including visits, security, and monitoring of his movements after the official letter had been received.

Najib, 73, was granted a conditional pardon by the Yang di-Pertuan Agong, Sultan Ibrahim, on Friday, allowing him to serve the remainder of his prison sentence in the SRC International case under house arrest until Aug 23, 2028, subject to payment of his RM50 million fine and other conditions.
The Agong presides over meetings of the Federal Territories Pardons Board, which comprises the attorney-general, the federal territories minister, and three members appointed by him.

The legal affairs division of the Prime Minister’s Department said Najib must comply with all the conditions imposed, failing which the conditional pardon would be revoked. It did not provide details of the conditions.

Najib was imprisoned in August 2022 after the Federal Court upheld his conviction for abuse of power, criminal breach of trust and money laundering involving RM42 million belonging to SRC International, a former subsidiary of 1MDB.

He had been serving a reduced six-year prison sentence at Kajang prison after the FTPB halved his original 12-year sentence in February 2024. The initial RM210 million fine was also reduced to RM50 million.
fc3205bad1ecd30c: NICE, Sept 20 — The widower of French screen icon Brigitte Bardot on Saturday slammed as a “joke” the planned auction of hundreds of the late star’s personal belongings organised by her animal welfare foundation.
The sale, featuring more than 300 items ranging from portraits and toiletries to a flamenco guitar and a black tutu, is due to take place Monday at Paris auction house Drouot.
“These are personal items. Why hold this sale? For the animals? It’s a joke,” Bernard d’Ormale told AFP, adding it amounted to a “disrespect to Brigitte’s memory”.
“All of this could have been kept for the day when people are able to visit La Madrague,” he added, referring to Bardot’s famed home in Saint-Tropez.
He said around three-quarters of the items came from Bardot’s Paris apartment, with the remainder from La Madrague.

Her belongings should have been preserved as part of her legacy rather than sold to raise funds for the foundation she created, d’Ormale argued, adding that Bardot “would not have agreed to this sale”.
The Brigitte Bardot Foundation rejected the criticism, saying the auction was approved by the board in June, including Bardot’s widower, who was then its president.

A visitor looks at items of personal belongings once owned by late French actress Brigitte Bardot displayed during a preview exhibition at Maison Drouot in Paris on September 15, 2026, ahead of an auction of her memorabilia and clothing. — AFP pic
However, d’Ormale said he had not understood the auction would involve such personal items.
The dispute comes days after he was removed as head of the foundation, a role he had held since the star’s death in December.
The 85-year-old, who remains on the foundation’s board, also complained he no longer has free access to La Madrague.
“I’ve lived there for 35 years and now they’re throwing me out. It’s quite something,” d’Ormale said.

Founded by the actor in 1986, the Brigitte Bardot Foundation says it has taken in 13,000 animals through four shelters and 150 partner facilities, supports 350 groups in France and operates in 70 countries. — AFP
81c2110d58a4dccc: KOTA TINGGI, Sept 20 — Anthony Loke’s offer to resign as Transport Minister following former prime minister Datuk Seri Najib Razak’s conditional pardon is entirely his own matter, Umno vice-president Datuk Seri Mohamed Khaled Nordin said today.

Loke offered to resign yesterday after DAP’s central executive committee meeting, saying the move was the party’s response to the decision allowing Najib to serve the remainder of his sentence under house arrest, while other DAP ministers would remain in the unity government to maintain political stability.

“From Umno’s perspective, that is his matter. Whether he wants to resign or not, that is his matter,” The Star quoted Khaled as replying to reporters after attending a Maulidur Rasul celebration at Felda Air Tawar 2 here.
Khaled, who is also defence minister, said Loke’s resignation offer should not be confused with the decision involving Najib.

Khaled reiterated that the decision to grant Najib a conditional pardon and allow him to serve the remainder of his sentence under house arrest was within the constitutional prerogative of the Yang di-Pertuan Agong.
He said Umno welcomed the decision and would respect the authority exercised by the King.
Loke said yesterday that DAP respected the Yang di-Pertuan Agong’s power to grant pardons but had its own position on Najib’s conditional pardon, which he said was difficult for the party to accept.
He said only he would offer to resign, while the other DAP ministers and deputy ministers would remain in government to ensure political stability.
Najib was granted a conditional pardon last Friday allowing him to serve the remainder of his sentence under house arrest until August 23, 2028, subject to payment of a RM50 million fine.

He has been serving a six-year prison sentence at Kajang Prison since August 2022 after the Federal Court upheld his conviction and 12-year jail term for misappropriating RM42 million from SRC International, with the sentence and fine later reduced by the Pardons Board in 2024.

d78905474687e96c: From Chin Yee Mun

According to demographic transition theory (DDT), birth rates are expected to decline as a society shifts from an agrarian to an industrial economy, with this change affecting the size and composition of its population.
In an agrarian society, birth rates are high but are also accompanied by high death rates. As a result, population growth was minimal in most societies at the time.
This began to change as societies moved towards industrial economies. Better healthcare meant lower death rates, while birth rates remained more or less unchanged.

However, this trend eventually began to change. Besides better healthcare, industrialisation brought urbanisation, improved education, modern lifestyles and, most importantly, changes in values. Individualism took root as industrialisation empowered such a culture.

As a result, birth rates began to decline. This is particularly visible among Malaysian Chinese. The decline in childbirth among the Chinese in Malaysia, as well as elsewhere, became apparent in the 1980s. The total fertility rate (TFR) among Malaysian Chinese women was 3.3 in 1980. Two decades later, it had fallen to 2.1.

According to the WHO, a TFR of 2.1 is generally considered the replacement level needed for a population to maintain its size over the long term, assuming no migration. If the TFR falls below this level, a population will eventually begin to shrink and age.
Unfortunately, the Chinese community’s TFR has continued to decline. Last year, the TFR among Chinese women was 0.8.

Reports from the statistics department show that the number of Malaysian Chinese has been declining since 2021. Migration is certainly one factor contributing to this decline, but the bigger factor is likely the fall in the Chinese birth rate.
In other words, the Chinese population is now at the “free-fall” stage. In DDT, this refers to a possible fifth stage.

According to the theory, some societies may see birth rates increase after the fourth stage, while others may continue to experience declines. Unfortunately, DDT describes these trends but does not explain why they occur.
Based on my analysis of the Chinese community in Malaysia, as well as Chinese communities across the Sinosphere, I believe I can offer an explanation.
For me, the Chinese have moved into hypermodernity. I took this term from Gilles Lipovetsky, who defined hypermodernity as an era characterised by the following:
Hyper-individualism: An intense focus on personal freedom, self-realisation and immediate gratification.
Hyper-consumerism: Consumption driven not only by status, but also by emotional experiences, health, wellness and constant novelty.
Hyper-technologisation: Technology operating at breakneck speed, redefining time, space and human interaction.

At present, particularly among younger Chinese people, hyper-individualism is increasingly evident. This can be observed in their lifestyles, including the pursuit of immediate gratification and an aversion to responsibilities. They are also driven by hyper-consumerism, sometimes consuming beyond their means.
Technology appears to reinforce these tendencies by connecting people while constantly exposing them to new products and experiences designed to provide gratification.
When such behaviour takes hold, values change.
Chinese values traditionally prioritised family, with starting a family often seen as a natural responsibility.

In a hypermodern world, however, this view is becoming less influential. Family can instead be perceived as a burden or an obstacle to personal gratification and the consumption of goods and experiences that provide satisfaction.

Hence, a subculture of anti-familism appears to be growing among Chinese youth. It may have been started by individuals who view the family as an institution that undermines happiness and life satisfaction.
This can be seen on social media, where various videos encourage singlehood and portray marriage as awful or destructive.
When such messages become widespread, they can validate the idea that it is acceptable to remain single, not start a family and not have children.

Hyper-consumerism may also contribute to the perception that raising children is financially unaffordable. For many Chinese families, raising a child is associated with spending on expensive preschools, private schools and universities.
While wanting to provide the best for one’s children is commendable, these expectations can also become a convenient justification for choosing not to have children.

This problem is now spreading to other communities in Malaysia. The Indian community faces a similar problem, with declining birth rates and a shrinking population. Similar trends are also emerging among Malays and the Bumiputera communities in Sabah and Sarawak.

In my view, measures to address or at least contain this problem must go beyond financial incentives. Many developing countries do not face the same low-birth-rate problem, while the issue is particularly pronounced in upper-middle-income and developed countries.
Hence, the problem is not simply about income. It is about the broader social ecology.

We need to bring hypermodernity under control by addressing hyper-individualism, hyper-consumerism and the influence of technology, particularly social media. At the same time, other measures could help create an environment that is more conducive to starting families and having children.
For example, childcare costs could be reduced by allowing childcare centres to operate in or near workplaces.

Tax and financial incentives could also be introduced as part of a broader effort to improve this social ecology, making it more conducive to forming families and having children rather than relying on them as the primary means of addressing the problem.
Chin Yee Mun is an associate professor and the director of the Tun Tan Cheng Lock Institute of Social Studies at Universiti Tunku Abdul Rahman.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

780abcb9ed5df790: SEPTEMBER 20 — We often think of dementia as a disease of forgetting. But sometimes, the first signs are not simply about memory. They can appear as small changes in everyday life — moments when things that were once familiar begin to feel a little less easy.

These changes can be subtle. A television remote they have used countless times may seem difficult to navigate, leaving them wondering why the TV is not working. A recipe they have followed for decades may become harder to follow, leading them to wonder whether something is wrong with the ingredients.

The same question may come up again and again in a conversation, without them realising it has already been answered. Because these changes can be gradual, they may easily be overlooked or simply put down to getting older.

We all have moments when we forget a name, lose our train of thought, or walk into a room and forget what we intended to do. Ageing, stress, tiredness, or other health conditions can affect memory and thinking.

Not every change means dementia, and these signs alone cannot confirm a diagnosis. But when these changes persist and begin to affect everyday life, they are worth noticing rather than simply being dismissed as normal ageing. Speaking to a healthcare professional can help determine what may be happening.
This World Alzheimer’s Month, the campaign carries a simple but important message: “The Earlier You Know, The More You Can Do: A Dementia Diagnosis Matters.”

Although dementia cannot currently be reversed or cured, an early diagnosis gives individuals and families more time to understand what is happening, explore available support and treatment options, and prepare for what lies ahead. It can also help the person living with dementia maintain independence and live as well as possible for as long as possible.

Dementia also affects the people who love and care for them. As dementia progresses, communication can become more difficult. A person may struggle to find the right words, follow a conversation or express what they need. For families and caregivers, adapting to these changes can be challenging.

When communication changes, we need to change the way we communicate — not the relationship. This might mean using simpler words, allowing more time for an answer, or offering reassurance instead of correcting.

The writer says early recognition of dementia can give individuals and families more time to understand the condition, explore support and treatment options, and prepare for what lies ahead. — Unsplash pic

It may mean finding a different way to approach a difficult moment and meeting where they are, rather than expecting them to communicate as they once did. Memories may fade, and dementia may change the conversation, but the need to feel loved, understood and connected remains.

This World Alzheimer’s Day, let’s start by noticing the changes and learning to listen differently. Because the earlier we know, the more we can do — for the person living with dementia, for the people who care for them, and for the relationships, choices, and moments that matter most.

518442fa7aa3e7d9: HONG KONG: Hong Kong officials and the public commemorated the city's first post-colonial leader, Tung Chee-hwa, at his funeral on Sunday, AFP journalists saw.
Tung, who died this month at the age of 89, was a former shipping tycoon hand-picked by Beijing to run Hong Kong after the former British colony's handover to Chinese rule in 1997.
The stauch conservative oversaw a rocky eight-year tenure until he resigned in 2005, following widespread protests.
Tung's casket, draped with the Chinese national flag, was driven in a hearse from the Hong Kong Funeral Home to a crematorium on Sunday, AFP reporters saw.
A portrait of Tung -- smiling and sporting his signature crew cut -- was displayed in the memorial hall, surrounded by white orchids symbolising love and respect.
Hundreds of wreaths sent by government officials and business leaders lined the street outside the memorial hall.
A tribute note from his alma mater, Britain's University of Liverpool, read: "We remember him with great gratitude and respect."
A divisive figure, Tung's policies set the tone for the city's development following the handover, with some sparking widespread protests.
A funeral committee hailed him as a "renowned patriot" and "close friend of the Communist Party".
Cheung Kwok-lik, an 89-year-old retired renovation worker, said he had travelled an hour by bus to pay his condolences to the former leader.
During his tenure, Tung weathered the Asian financial crisis and the deadly SARS epidemic, which "was by no means easy", Cheung said.
Tung's leadership also coincided with record unemployment and the 1997 avian flu outbreak.
Resident Kiki Ho said that even after paying her respects, she still felt "sorrowful and emotional".
"Given that era and circumstances he encountered, the situation was not in his favour," the 68-year-old said.
"He was a gentleman, a man of experience who genuinely wanted to do something for Hong Kong... but the political arena may have been too complicated for him," she added.
The British and US consulates had previously praised Tung for the historic role he played.
For decades, he served as an essential bridge connecting Beijing, Hong Kong and Washington.

Max Baucus, a former US ambassador to China who called Tung a close friend, said: "In the later decades of his life, he was devoted to the belief that our two countries... needed to assure and maintain mutual peace."
"He believed the best way to achieve that was through people-to-people diplomacy," Baucus added.
Tung is survived by his wife Betty Chiu, their two sons and their daughter.

945bafcf6aecf6d0: KUALA LUMPUR: Artificial intelligence (AI) should not be seen as a replacement for human intelligence but as a powerful tool that can extend creativity, productivity and human potential.

Internet marketing company Artisense Online Sdn Bhd director Sheena Lai said AI could generate ideas and complete tasks quickly, but human creativity remained rooted in emotions, experiences, memories and personal perspectives.
"Creativity is not simply about producing something new. It is about seeing something differently," she said.
Lai said AI could help overcome a creative block by offering multiple ideas and possible directions, but it could not determine which idea was personally meaningful.
"AI can give us 10 ideas in seconds, but it cannot decide which idea actually means something to us," she said.
She said people should also remain critical of AI-generated content as the technology could produce inaccurate or vague information while sounding confident.
"That is precisely why human judgment matters more today, not less," she said.
Lai likened AI to technological tools that had transformed how people worked without making human skills obsolete.
"A calculator did not make mathematicians useless, and a camera did not make artists obsolete," she said.
She said the same principle applied to AI, which should be used to complement rather than replace human thinking.
"The smartest people are not turning their brains off for AI. They are steering AI with intention instead of trying to compete against it," she said.
Lai said AI could provide endless possibilities, while humans brought purpose, emotion and individual perspectives to the creative process.
"AI can provide endless possibilities, but humans bring the essential purpose, the authentic feeling and the human point of view," she said.
She said the key was not choosing between the human brain and AI, but knowing how to use both effectively.
"Use your brain, use your imagination and experience, and use the AI next to you when it helps.
"Let AI do what it does best. And let humans do what only humans can do — decide what is worth creating," she said.
Lastly, she posed a question at the heart of the debate over AI and creativity: 'Was this content created by her or by AI?'

6cbb035ec1dd5f6a: Sejak kebelakangan ini, media sosial dibanjiri dengan pelbagai bentuk gangguan, ancaman, malah ugutan secara terang-terangan terhadap penjawat awam di Negeri Sembilan yang berpegang teguh pada Perlembagaan. Mari kita perjelaskan satu hakikat asas sebelum mereka ini terus berhalusinasi bahawa kononnya boleh memanipulasi, memaksa, atau membuli penjawat awam demi permainan politik mereka.

Setiap penjawat awam di negara ini menggalas sumpah keramat. Mereka bersumpah setia kepada raja dan negara, berikrar untuk memelihara, melindungi, dan mempertahankan perlembagaan serta menegakkan kedaulatan undang-undang. Mereka sama sekali tidak bersumpah setia kepada kehendak nafsu, tuntutan haram, atau desakan politik mana-mana pihak, individu yang berkuasa, mahupun penderhaka yang begitu agresif.

Tindakan memaksa, menekan, mengganggu, dan mengugut penjawat awam untuk melaksanakan perkara yang sangat jelas melanggar undang-undang dan Perlembagaan adalah sesuatu yang amat mengejutkan. Seriuslah? Adakah pihak-pihak tertentu ini sudah hilang akal, atau mereka menganggap diri mereka mengatasi kedaulatan undang-undang?

<0>Penjawat awam bukannya catur yang boleh diperkotak-katikkan tanpa sebarang perlindungan. Mereka dilindungi sepenuhnya oleh undang-undang daripada sebarang bentuk gangguan, ugutan, dan paksaan yang melanggar undang-undang. Mana-mana pihak yang cuba berlagak samseng terhadap penjawat awam sepatutnya meneliti Kanun Keseksaan dengan sedalam-dalamnya sebelum melangkah lebih jauh:

Menakutkan secara jenayah (Seksyen 503 & 506 Kanun Keseksaan): Mengugut atau menakutkan penjawat awam untuk memaksa mereka bertindak di luar bidang kuasa undang-undang merupakan satu kesalahan menakutkan secara jenayah. Jika sabit kesalahan, pesalah boleh dipenjarakan antara dua hingga tujuh tahun, didenda berat, atau kedua-duanya sekali.

Mengugut penjawat awam (Seksyen 189 Kanun Keseksaan): Mengancam untuk mendatangkan bencana kepada penjawat awam—atau mana-mana pihak yang mempunyai kepentingan dengannya (seperti ahli keluarga)—bagi memaksa atau menghalang mereka daripada menjalankan tugas rasmi membawa hukuman penjara sehingga dua tahun, denda, atau kedua-duanya.

Subversi perlembagaan & rampasan kuasa (Seksyen 121B Kanun Keseksaan): Percubaan memaksa penjawat awam melanggar Perlembagaan Persekutuan atau negeri merupakan cabaran secara langsung terhadap kedaulatan raja Melayu. Tindakan mencabar pihak berkuasa yang bernaung di bawah Yang di-Pertuan Agong atau raja-raja Melayu membawa hukuman berat sehingga penjara seumur hidup.
Adakah mereka benar-benar terlupa bahawa penjawat awam kita dilindungi di bawah peruntukan undang-undang yang ketat ini daripada taktik kotor, gangguan, dan ugutan?
Negeri Sembilan sebagai sebuah negeri dalam persekutuan

Bukan itu sahaja, di bawah Perkara 145 Perlembagaan Persekutuan, peguam negara (AG) merupakan penasihat undang-undang utama bagi seluruh persekutuan. Jabatan Peguam Negara (AGC) bertanggungjawab memberikan nasihat undang-undang kepada kerajaan persekutuan dan kerajaan-kerajaan Negeri di seluruh Semenanjung. Sejak bila pula AGC dilarang atau dikecualikan daripada memberikan pandangan undang-undang berhubung pelanggaran Perlembagaan yang serius yang berlaku di mana-mana negeri di Malaysia? Amat dangkal jika ada pihak yang mendakwa bahawa kononnya jentera perundangan persekutuan tidak boleh campur tangan atau memberi nasihat apabila Perlembagaan dikoyak-koyakkan di peringkat negeri—ini satu penghinaan terhadap struktur asas Perlembagaan kita.

Negeri Sembilan ialah sebuah negeri yang sah dalam Persekutuan Malaysia. Negeri Sembilan bukannya sebuah wilayah autonomi, dan jauh sekali daripada merupakan satu wilayah tanpa apa-apa penguatkuasaan undang-undang, di mana paksaan ke atas pelanggaran perlembagaan boleh pula menggantikan kedaulatan undang-undang. Mana-mana pihak yang cuba memaksa penjawat awam di Negeri Sembilan—atau di mana-mana jua dalam negara ini—untuk bertindak melanggar undang-undang secara langsung adalah melakukan kesalahan terhadap perlembagaan negeri, kerajaan persekutuan, dan ke atas Kebawah Duli Yang Maha Mulia Seri Paduka Baginda Yang di-Pertuan Agong selaku ketua kegara bagi persekutuan.

Apa yang menjadikan keseluruhan tindakan ini lebih memalukan adalah betapa asingnya ia daripada jiwa Negeri Sembilan itu sendiri. Kempen paksaan, gertakan, dan subversi luar perlembagaan oleh golongan penderhaka ini merupakan satu serangan langsung terhadap semangat Adat Perpatih. Dibangunkan atas tiang seri adab, saling menghormati, ketertiban, serta kepatuhan mutlak kepada aturan adat dan undang-undang, Adat Perpatih langsung tidak memberi ruang kepada taktik samseng yang membelakangkan hukum dan undang-undang. Mengganggu dan memaksa penjawat awam melanggar undang-undang di Negeri Sembilan bukan sahaja satu jenayah Perlembagaan—bahkan ia adalah perbuatan yang benar-benar un-adat yang mencemarkan warisan suci bumi ini.

Kepada penjawat awam kita yang berdedikasi di Negeri Sembilan: kekal berkhidmat, berdiri teguh, dan pertahankan pendirian anda. Jangan berganjak walau seinci jua pun kepada tekanan haram, ancaman, atau tekanan politik. Anda sedang menjalankan tugas yang sah, dan perlembagaan berdiri teguh sebagai perisai anda. Kepada seluruh warga perkhidmatan awam di Malaysia: bersatulah dalam solidariti utuh bersama rakan sekerja di Negeri Sembilan. Ancaman terhadap integriti perundangan terhadap penjawat awam di Negeri Sembilan adalah serangan ke atas perkhidmatan awam seluruhnya!
Sikap biadab dan ketidakpatuhan undang-undang ini sudah melampaui batas.

Kepada Polis Diraja Malaysia (PDRM) dan pihak berkuasa penegak undang-undang: mohon bertindak pantas dan tegas terhadap dalang-dalang ini. Siasat setiap ancaman, tegakkan peruntukan Kanun Keseksaan tanpa rasa gentar atau pilih kasih, dan pertahankan kedaulatan undang-undang negara kita.
Kedaulatan undang-undang tidak boleh dikompromi. Penjawat awam tidak akan dibuli, dan negara ini tidak akan bertolak kompromi dengan sebarang bentuk subversi di siang hari.
Artikel ini adalah pandangan penulis dan tidak semestinya mewakili FMT.
52164dbf9a53cd4a: PETALING JAYA: PAS election director Sanusi Nor has mocked DAP’s decision for only its secretary-general, Loke Siew Fook, to resign from the Cabinet over former prime minister Najib Razak’s conditional pardon, describing it as “firecracker politics”.
Sanusi compared the move with housing and local government minister Nga Kor Ming’s previous announcement that he would resign, although he ultimately did not.
The Kedah menteri besar said DAP’s latest move showed that the party frequently flip-flopped on its political decisions.
“Nga said the same thing before. He didn’t resign either. They act as if they’re going to take action, but nothing gets done. It’s firecracker politics. Lots of noise, then silence,” he told FMT.
“DAP plays flip-flop politics. Next, they’ll find an excuse not to resign. Before this, they said they wanted to leave the government. Then they found an excuse not to.”
After a three-hour DAP central executive committee meeting yesterday, Loke, who is the transport minister, announced that he would resign from the Cabinet.
The decision followed calls for DAP to take broader action, including leaving the government, over Najib's conditional pardon.
Loke described his resignation as a “responsible” move and said DAP would remain in the government.

Najib, 73, was granted a conditional pardon by the Yang di-Pertuan Agong on Friday, allowing him to serve the remainder of his prison sentence in the SRC International case under house arrest until Aug 23, 2028, subject to payment of his RM50 million fine and other conditions.

The legal affairs division of the Prime Minister’s Department said Najib must comply with all the conditions imposed, failing which the conditional pardon would be revoked. It did not provide details of the conditions.

Najib was imprisoned in August 2022 after the Federal Court upheld his conviction for abuse of power, criminal breach of trust and money laundering involving RM42 million belonging to SRC International, a former subsidiary of 1MDB.

He has been serving a reduced six-year sentence at Kajang prison after the Federal Territories Pardons Board halved his original 12-year sentence in February 2024. His initial RM210 million fine was also reduced to RM50 million.
6a6b54bb33e4072b: GEORGE TOWN: The Consumers' Association of Penang (CAP) has urged the government to raise cigarette sales tax in 2027 Budget to curb smoking among young people.
CAP senior education officer and anti-smoking activist N. V. Subbarow said the measure was needed amid concerns over smoking among secondary and primary school students.
He said new statistics showed 43,019 secondary school students and 341 primary school students were smoking cigarettes.
"This is not good for a healthy country," he said today.

Subbarow said Malaysia already had about five million smokers and 1.5 million vapers, adding that higher cigarette prices could make tobacco products less affordable and discourage young people from taking up smoking.
"CAP feels that it is high time for a mandatory sales tax on cigarettes," he added.

He said higher cigarette prices could also encourage smokers to quit or cut down, while reducing smoking could lower government spending on treating smoking-related diseases, which he put at about RM16 billion annually.
"The prime minister, who is also finance minister, must consider the health of the future generation," he said.

160e56a5a66d6fe3: CAPAS: Tribal leader Petronila Munoz walked across the sweeping Philippine grasslands she has called home for generations, uncertain about its future, as a sprawling tech hub for a US-led initiative takes shape.

With little information and no prior consultation, the Indigenous chieftain said her Aeta Hungey tribe was uncertain how much of their land could be affected or what will become of the livelihood it provides.
"There's still no clarity," Munoz told AFP inside the tribe's traditional meeting hall.
"What will happen to us? That's our biggest question."

In April, the US announced that the Philippines had joined Pax Silica, a US-led effort to strengthen supply chains for semiconductors and rare earth elements and reduce participating countries' dependence on China.

The Philippines has designated a 1,620-hectare site in New Clark City in Tarlac province, north of Manila, for a manufacturing hub aimed at producing high-end components for use in artificial intelligence data centres.
The government estimates the initiative could attract up to US$70 billion in investment and create about 190,000 jobs, a major boost to a country with more than three million unemployed people.
The project has a long timeline. No tenants have been confirmed.
Plans to domestically process the country's mineral resources could be even further away.
For about 1,000 Aetas, however, the prospect of displacement is already here.
In July, they received a letter from the Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) warning that the project "could affect your occupied lands".
'Money runs out'

Munoz said visiting BCDA employees told them to leave by December and relocate to an area about 16km from their current home, without providing a master plan showing which parts of their ancestral domains would be affected.
Munoz said the BCDA has offered them just 30 pesos (US$0.48) per square metre for their lands, an offer all declined.
"Our lives, our livelihood and our culture are tied to this ancestral land," Munoz said.
"Land is more important. Money runs out."
The BCDA declined to address specific questions about the Aetas' situation and rejected a freedom of information request for the site's official boundary map and geospatial data.
It said the information was being "withheld temporarily until the official action is finalised or published".
At a Senate hearing last month, BCDA president Joshua Bingcang said the Aetas were living on government land. Like many Indigenous groups in the Philippines, they hold no land title.
Civic groups have also raised concerns about the project's environmental impact, particularly the demand for water and electricity in a country plagued by droughts and rotational power outages.
The US Statement Department told AFP that "environmental, water, energy, and community-impact studies" would inform the project's design.
"Before any major development happens, we expect rigorous stakeholder impact assessments will take place," a spokesman said.
Bingcang told the Senate that investors would be required to build their own power and water systems.
'We have to open up'

Alvin Camba, research director at an AI firm focused on supply chains and risk assessment, said Manila's close relationship with the United States could motivate investors to set up shop despite the power concerns.
Last month, reports said Washington planned to warn countries they could be excluded from Pax Silica if they joined a rival framework backed by Beijing.

"This is where the advantage of the Philippines comes in. The Philippines is the least affected by Chinese capital in Southeast Asia," Camba told AFP, saying the country would offer foreign companies the ability to "disentangle" from China.
For political economist Calixto Chikiamco, Pax Silica represents a "historic opportunity" for the Philippines to move beyond its traditional wheelhouse of microchip testing and packaging.
"We have to open up to foreign investment so that technology transfer (to the Philippines) will happen," he told AFP.
Sacrifices
The BCDA has been conducting public consultations in Tarlac and nearby provinces, but the agency has yet to hold talks with her tribe, Munoz said.
The Aetas remain uncertain if the government would help them build new homes or provide land to cultivate for income if they are moved.
"I wish they would listen to us. They're just talking among themselves," she said, adding she worried her tribe would not be qualified for the sort of new jobs Pax Silica promised.
While a proponent of the initiative, Chikiamco said the government was doing "a terrible job" explaining the benefits and tradeoffs it represented.
Camba agreed: "I would actually advise the Philippine government to be very transparent about what's happening. A big problem is transparency."
Still, the benefits outweigh the risks, he said.
"Every country that has... jump-started development has had to make sacrifices," Camba said.
But 63-year-old Munoz, who hopes to be buried in her tribe's traditional burial ground, said she would not leave, even if a backhoe flattened her home.
"Why do we have to be the ones to sacrifice for the kind of development they want?" she asked.
2dc38a5290d40ea3: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 20 — Indonesian actress Dian Sastrowardoyo has spent more than two decades building a career across film and television, with roles that have made her one of the country’s most recognisable actresses.

Audiences might recognise her in films such as 2001’s Whispering Sands and What’s Up with Love?, as well as the more recent Netflix series Cigarette Girl, which won outstanding web series at the 2024 Bandung Film Festival.
Her connection with Malaysian cinema also goes back more than two decades, beginning with a cameo in Saw Teong Hin’s 2004 film Puteri Gunung Ledang, which starred Tiara Jacquelina and Datuk M. Nasir.
More recently, Dian returned to Malaysia to work with filmmaker Woo Ming Jin on the Malaysia-Indonesia production The Fox King, this time in a leading role.
The film, which was released in Malaysian cinemas on September 17, sees Dian play Lara, an English teacher, alongside Malaysian actors Idan Aedan and Hadi Putra.

Speaking during a recent media session at TintaBudi Bookshop in TTDI Plaza, Dian described making the film as a short but enjoyable experience, saying she quickly fell in love with the script before preparing for and filming the project within just a few weeks.
The production also meant spending time away from her family during the fasting month as she travelled to Malaysia for filming.
Hoping for The Fox King Indonesia rollout soon

The Fox King has since travelled the international festival circuit, with screenings at the Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF) and Busan International Film Festival before arriving in Malaysian cinemas.
For Dian, the next step is seeing whether the film can also reach Indonesian audiences.
Speaking to Malay Mail, she said she hoped the film would eventually be screened in Indonesian cinemas.
“I hope it can be played in cinemas in Indonesia because it hasn’t got the chance to be played in the cinemas.
“There are so many films that want to go to the cinemas, and I think The Fox King is also in the queue to go to the cinema,” she said.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Dian Sastrowardoyo (centre) during a media session at TintaBudi Bookshop in TTDI Plaza, with Finas CEO Datuk Azmir Saifuddin Mutalib also present. — Picture courtesy of Kuman Pictures
More Malaysia-Indonesia collaborations
Acknowledging the recent wave of Malaysia-Indonesia collaborations, Dian welcomed the growing exchange between Malaysian and Indonesian filmmakers and actors.
She said greater collaboration between the two countries would allow both industries to learn from one another.
“I think it’s really fantastic that the collaborations are happening so fast.
“I think it should happen more and more.
“I am looking forward to more opportunities to work with Malaysian filmmakers, and I’m looking forward to Malaysian filmmakers collaborating more and more with Indonesian filmmakers.
“I think in order to grow and learn together, we need to have a lot of collaborations.”

Dian said the exchange could also create more opportunities for actors from both countries, pointing to Malaysian actors Chew Kin Wah and Bront Palarae as examples of Malaysian talent finding roles across the border.
“So many stories are being filmed, so many stories are being told, so we need to collaborate,” she said.
Acting and seeing life from different perspectives
Looking back at her career, Dian said acting had also changed the way she viewed herself and the people around her.
“I think I learned a lot by becoming an actor.
“I think becoming an actor makes me very observant as a person, and I learn more about my own character,” she said.
“Growing up, there is a lot of growing that happens in your character.
“You become more dewasa (mature), right? I think by becoming an actor, you can take so many angles and points of view that enrich your own.”
She said taking on different characters and perspectives had allowed her to better understand people while also encouraging her to reflect on her own character as she continued to grow.
Looking ahead
Dian said she remained open to working with more Malaysian filmmakers, describing her experience with Woo on The Fox King as an enjoyable one.
She also spoke fondly of the late Malaysian filmmaker Yasmin Ahmad and her work, while expressing interest in collaborating more with filmmaker Amir Muhammad.
Currently, Dian already has more work in the pipeline, including The Sea Speaks His Name, an upcoming Indonesian political drama also starring Reza Rahadian.
The film is set to have its world premiere in the competition section of the 31st Busan International Film Festival next month.
For now, Dian hopes Malaysian audiences will head to cinemas to experience The Fox King, which is currently screening nationwide.
1e5d50101428c018: WORLD leaders gather in New York every September for several days of high-level debate starting on Tuesday at the United Nations General Assembly.
The United Nations was formed in 1945 with 51 original members and has since grown to 193 members.
Leaders of two non-member observer states – known at the UN as the Holy See and the State of Palestine – and an observer member, the European Union, can also speak.
This month marks the start of the 81st session.

It is tradition for Brazil to always be the first member state to speak. This is because in the early years of the world body Brazil stepped up to speak first when other countries were reluctant to do so, say UN officials.
As host to the UN headquarters in New York, the United States is the second country to address the General Assembly.
From there the list is then based on hierarchy and generally on a first-come, first-served basis.
Heads of state speak first, followed by deputy heads of state and crown princes, heads of government, ministers and lower-ranking heads of a delegation.
HOW LONG WILL THEY SPEAK?
Leaders are asked to stick to a voluntary 15-minute time limit.
According to UN records, one of the longest speeches made during the opening of a General Assembly was in 1960 by Cuban leader Fidel Castro who spoke for about 4-1/2 hours.
Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi spoke for more than 1-1/2 hours in 2009.
WHAT WILL THEY TALK ABOUT?
Each start of a General Assembly session has a theme. Leaders might briefly refer to the theme before moving on to whatever topic they like.
This year's theme is: "Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations That Delivers for All."
Other topics that leaders are likely to address and discuss in meetings on the sidelines of the General Assembly include:
ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE.

The high-level General Assembly will convene just weeks after several AI industry leaders called for a coordinated slowdown of the development of the increasingly powerful technology, warning that it could soon improve on its own and slip beyond human control.

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said on Wednesday the warnings cannot be ignored and that AI would be a major topic of his discussions with world leaders next week, telling reporters that countries on the frontiers of AI needed to communicate and establish "common guardrails in order to avoid this race to the bottom that could lead one day to a gigantic disaster at the global level."
The UN Security Council may meet next week on AI, diplomats said. The 15-member council met for the first time on artificial intelligence in 2023.
IRAN
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is scheduled to address the General Assembly on Wednesday, seven months after the United States and Israel went to war with Teheran.
However, his travel to New York appears uncertain.
Abbas Mousavi, Pezeshkian's chief of protocol, said on Monday it was still unclear how many members of the Iranian delegation would be issued visas by the United States and when.

While US President Donald Trump, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the leaders of several countries involved in trying to mediate an end to the war will also be at the United Nations next week, a breakthrough in the stalled diplomacy is unlikely.
The UN Security Council may hold an informal meeting with Arab leaders next week, diplomats said, at which Iran is expected to be the key topic of discussion.
UKRAINE
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy will be seeking to shore up global support for Kyiv as Trump tries to broker an end to the war more than four years after Russia invaded its neighbour.
He is due to address the assembly on Wednesday while Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov will speak on Saturday.
The UN Security Council is also expected to hold a high-level meeting on Ukraine next week. It has been unable to take any action to try to end the war as Russia is a veto power.
Trump has at times appeared frustrated that he has been unable to broker an end to the war, a goal he declared a priority when he began his second term in January last year.
The US president spoke with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin earlier this month, but it is unclear if he plans to meet Zelenskyy in New York.
ISRAEL/PALESTINIANS

Israel's Netanyahu – wanted by the International Criminal Court for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, which Israel denies – is due to address the General Assembly on Thursday next week.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani believes Netanyahu should be arrested, but said in July he lacked the legal authority.
Mamdani said on Wednesday he had no plans to attend any anti-Netanyahu protests next week, but that he respected the right of New Yorkers to demonstrate.
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas will not attend the General Assembly in person. The United States, a close Israeli ally, has again said it will not give him a visa.
He is likely to appear via video – also on Thursday – as he did last year.

There is also likely to be a high-level meeting on the sidelines of the General Assembly next week to promote a two-state solution between Israel and the Palestinians, diplomats said, but no progress toward that goal is expected.
RACE TO APPOINT A NEW UN SECRETARY-GENERAL
The United Nations has started the process of choosing a new secretary-general, but there is no clear frontrunner.
Guterres will finish his second five-year term on December 31, 2026. There is likely to be chatter on the sidelines of the General Assembly next week about who should replace him.

The UN Security Council has to agree on a candidate to recommend to the 193-member General Assembly for election, which means the five council veto powers – Britain, China, France, Russia and the US – have to agree.
SUDAN
There is likely to be a high-level meeting on the conflict in Sudan on the sidelines of the General Assembly, diplomats said.

Sudan's war, which erupted in April 2023 following a power struggle between the military and the Rapid Support Forces, has displaced more than 14 million people and created one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, head of the Sudanese army and head of state after the overthrow of veteran leader Omar al-Bashir in 2019, is due to address the General Assembly on Thursday.
CLIMATE

As the world struggles to limit warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels – as agreed in the 2015 Paris ​climate agreement – leaders of smaller island nations and other states most affected by climate change are expected to again urge action.
August was the first month since November 2025 in which ​the world's average temperature exceeded 1.5 C.

f7a5359f8472aec0: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 20 — Datuk Seri Najib Razak’s move from prison to house arrest has yet to get the formal green light from the Malaysian Prisons Department, which says it is still waiting for official written notification of the conditional pardon granted to the former prime minister.

“In this regard, in line with the statement by Datuk Seri Saifuddin Nasution smail, Minister of Home Affairs on September 19, 2026, the Home Ministry and Malaysian Prisons Department are still awaiting official written notification regarding the decision before any further action to implement the decision can be determined.

The conditional royal pardon allows him to serve the remainder of that sentence under house arrest, but the RM50 million fine remains among the conditions attached to the decision.

d223c218f747a8c6: NAGOYA: International Olympic Committee (IOC) president Kirsty Coventry called the shipping container-style huts for Asian Games athletes "beautiful" on Sunday – but conceded they were "a little tighter" than similar accommodation at the Milan-Cortina Winter Olympics.
Asia's biggest sporting spectacle, which opened on Saturday in the Japanese city of Nagoya, has split with past Games by having no traditional athletes' village.
To save costs, the more than 17,000 Asian Games participants will stay in temporary huts, hotels and a cruise ship.
Some countries have criticised the wooden cabins as too small, with beds that are too short.
But after touring the lodgings, IOC president Coventry said she could not understand the negativity.
"We had similar cabins in Milan-Cortina (Winter Games this year) and the athletes were very happy. And the cabins here are really nice," said the Zimbabwean former Olympic champion swimmer.
"They're a little tighter. So, you know, if you want something negative, it's a little smaller.
"But I don't think it's a negative thing. I love the village."
About 2,000 participants are staying in the lodgings by the water in Nagoya.
Coventry said: "The cabins are quiet, they're very cool. The air conditioning is working well.
"The flooring and the walls are beautiful. It's better than some of the villages I've stayed in.
"So I think to be very fair to Japan and to the organising committee, I was really impressed.
"I had only been reading everything that had been said. And I was expecting something completely different to when I walked in."
Asked by AFP if she would happily see the temporary cabins and also a cruise ship serve as accommodation at the Olympics, she said she had not been to the vessel.
But she pointed to the accommodation at Milan-Cortina, and said those "very closely" resembled the ones in Nagoya.
"It's not a new concept," she added.
"And it is a concept that I think, for me, when we talk about an athlete experience, being an athlete... as soon as I go in, I'm not necessarily concerned about the look." - AFP

21592544911e0a7b: NAGOYA: Warnings of a typhoon partly explained why the Asian Games opening ceremony in Nagoya took place in front of thousands of empty seats, organisers said Sunday.
Saturday's gala at the 30,000-capacity stadium officially launched the continent's premier sporting event, with Japan's emperor and empress in attendance.
Fireworks brought the show to a rousing conclusion, but while parts of the arena were full, others were noticeably devoid of people.
Olympic Council of Asia director general Husain Al-Musallam said they had to keep one block empty because of the Games flame.
"This is one part," he told reporters, adding that more than 70% of tickets were sold.
That contrasted with an announcement at the Paloma Mizuho Stadium that said the ceremony was sold out.
"But maybe if you remember, it was a typhoon warning coming to Nagoya and at the last minute the typhoon shifted," Al-Musallam added.
"So the same question I've been asked, what happens if the typhoon is coming? That could affect the situation."
There was no rain during the ceremony, as the storm that had threatened the Games days earlier shifted its impact towards the Tokyo region.
There was heavy rain there on Sunday, where some Games events are being hosted -- notably the swimming -- with possible wet weather forecast for Nagoya later Sunday and Monday.
6452a958cd4209d6: PETALING JAYA: Jabatan Penjara Malaysia masih menunggu pemakluman rasmi secara bertulis berhubung keputusan pengampunan bersyarat terhadap bekas perdana menteri Najib Razak sebelum tindakan lanjut diambil.

Katanya, pemakluman dan dokumen rasmi berkaitan keputusan Lembaga Pengampunan Wilayah Persekutuan (LPWP) akan disampaikan melalui saluran rasmi sebelum dikemukakan kepada Jabatan Penjara untuk tindakan selanjutnya.

“Sehubungan itu, selaras kenyataan Saifuddin Nasution Ismail, menteri dalam negeri pada 19 Sept 2026, Kementerian Dalam Negeri dan Jabatan Penjara Malaysia masih menunggu pemakluman rasmi secara bertulis berhubung keputusan tersebut sebelum sebarang tindakan lanjut bagi melaksanakan keputusan berkenaan dapat ditentukan,” katanya dalam kenyataan.
Pada 18 Sept lalu, LPWP membenarkan Najib menjalani baki hukuman penjara di bawah tahanan rumah sehingga 23 Ogos 2028 menerusi pengampunan bersyarat.
Keputusan itu tertakluk kepada pembayaran denda RM50 juta serta pematuhan terhadap syarat ditetapkan.
Sementara itu, Jabatan Penjara berkata pihaknya sentiasa bersedia melaksanakan arahan rasmi yang diterima daripada pihak berkuasa berkaitan.
Katanya, pelaksanaan itu akan dibuat selaras peruntukan undang-undang, peraturan penjara serta tatacara dan prosedur yang sedang berkuat kuasa.

“Jabatan ini akan melaksanakan sebarang keputusan dan arahan yang diterima secara teratur, profesional dan berintegriti, selaras dengan peruntukan undang-undang serta ketetapan pihak berkuasa yang berkenaan,” katanya.
Jabatan Penjara turut menyeru semua pihak merujuk sumber rasmi dan tidak membuat spekulasi mengenai pelaksanaan keputusan berkenaan.

295a8b19057035e8: SIBU, Sept 20 — The Sarawak government has agreed in principle to an initial RM1.5 billion allocation to establish the Sibu Economic Zone (SEZ) as a dedicated platform to coordinate and shape the city’s economic development.
Deputy Premier Datuk Amar Dr Sim Kui Hian said the SEZ would focus on investment, the service sector and high-value employment.

“Sibu’s development will also be supported by stronger connectivity and industrial capacity, including the proposed West Bank Bridge and the Sibu Industrial Park, which is scheduled for completion in 2029.

“The proposed Bukit Assek redevelopment, which has received in-principle approval, is another important long-term initiative aimed at moving Sibu towards a more sustainable and higher-value economic direction,” he said at the Association of Chinese Chambers of Commerce and Industry of Sarawak (ACCCIS) annual general meeting here.
Also present was ACCCIS president Kong Chiong Ung.

Dr Sim said ACCCIS and its affiliated chambers had over the years provided an important platform for business networking, policy dialogue, capacity building and engagement between the government and business community.

The State Public health, Housing and Local Government Minister said the business community had an important role in Sarawak’s development, adding that the government valued the contribution of chambers such as ACCCIS in conveying businesses’ views and concerns.

“I encourage ACCCIS to continue serving as a constructive bridge between the government and the business community, particularly in identifying practical issues affecting businesses and contributing ideas towards Sarawak’s economic development,” he said.
Dr Sim said the private sector had an important role in turning policies, infrastructure and development platforms into actual investment, business activity and employment.
“Government development alone cannot achieve the full potential of Sibu or Sarawak. This is why organisations such as ACCCIS remain important partners to the government.”
He said the government would continue providing policy direction, infrastructure and platforms for growth, while businesses must be prepared to invest, innovate and identify new opportunities.
He also encouraged ACCCIS to continue bringing together businesses from across Sarawak and strengthening cooperation among its affiliated chambers.
“Through closer government-business collaboration, we can build a stronger, more resilient and more competitive Sarawak economy.”
D Sim also commended ACCCIS for extending its contribution beyond business advocacy, particularly through initiatives promoting environmental awareness, resource recycling and sustainable living.

He said the ‘How to Retain the Blue Sky Eco-Enzyme Public Workshop’ in 2024 and ‘How to Retain the Blue Sky 2.0: Five Eco Enzyme Lessons’ in 2026 demonstrated ACCCIS’ continued commitment to environmental sustainability.
He said the second workshop in June also saw eco-enzyme initiatives extended to schools to encourage environmental awareness among students.

“These initiatives are aligned with Sarawak’s Post Covid-19 Development Strategy 2030, which places economic prosperity, social inclusivity and environmental sustainability as the three key dimensions of Sarawak’s development vision.”

Dr Sim said environmental protection was not only an ecological responsibility but was increasingly connected to the future economy, including green industries, renewable energy and new high-value opportunities.

Looking forward, he said Sarawak was entering an important phase of economic transformation and must continue moving beyond traditional industries while developing new economic sectors, knowledge and technical capabilities.
He identified renewable and green energy, semiconductors, healthcare, digitalisation and technology-related industries as key areas for future growth.
Dr Sim also commended ACCCIS for launching its Digital Membership Database Management System yesterday.

“This is a positive step that shows ACCCIS is embracing digitalisation and moving in the same direction as Sarawak’s broader transformation towards a more digital and technology-driven economy,” he said. — The Borneo Post
2f98e325f66efb8e: PHILADELPHIA: Pop star Ed Sheeran said Saturday the situation in Gaza is "unjustifiable," following a wave of criticism that he had failed to back his opening act who was booted from the tour after making pro-Palestinian comments.
The singer, who had previously maintained an apolitical stance, broke his silence on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict in his first show since the controversy involving US rapper Macklemore.
"What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic and unjustifiable and disproportionate," Sheeran said in Philadelphia.
"Our hearts have been broken by the scale of devastation and loss of civilians' lives, children's lives, and the systemic injustice we're seeing unfold in the West Bank cannot be overlooked."
Macklemore had declared "Free Palestine" at a New Jersey concert this month, drawing backlash from owners of US stadiums hosting future dates of Sheeran's Loop Tour.
The British artist, 35, has denied being behind the decision to remove the rapper, instead blaming the tour promoter.
Four supporting acts subsequently walked out on the "Shape of You" singer, issuing public statements citing their support for Palestinians.
"I've had to take and make difficult decisions, and I am making mistakes, and I'm so so sorry," an emotional Sheeran told his audience, who responded with cheers.
Sheeran had been accused by critics of failing to stand up to the stadium owners – led by billionaire businessman Robert Kraft – and was targeted by boycott calls.
The singer said he was "deeply worried" about the idea of venues pre-approving the content of performances.
"This happens in so many places that I perform around the world, but it should never happen in the free world."
Boycott
A few dozen pro-Palestinian protesters rallied peacefully outside Lincoln Financial Field ahead of the concert, waving Palestinian flags and chanting "Free, free Palestine."
Some of the fans streaming into the stadium said they had hesitated about coming due to the controversy, but ultimately decided to attend and enjoy the music.
But others like Brandon Ateke changed their plans.
The 18-year-old Brown University student accused Sheeran of "complicity" with Kraft and others in silencing Macklemore.
"I decided to not attend the concert and instead attend the protest to bring light to the genocide going on in Gaza today," he told AFP.
On Saturday, a pro-Palestinian group urged artists, fans and crew members to stay away from Sheeran's concerts.

"We now extend our call for boycotting Ed Sheeran's entire world tour, including the upcoming Latin American dates, and the as-yet-unannounced European leg," the Palestinian Campaign for the Academic and Cultural Boycott of Israel (PACBI) said.
Solo
Sheeran started his show Saturday night alone on stage, without an opening act.
He later brought on five musicians who he said had learned his songs in three days, thanking them for joining him "in a week when no one wants to stand on stage with me."
The groups that quit the tour included Sheeran's backing band as well as performer Finneas, who rose to fame collaborating with his pop superstar sister Billie Eilish.

Since Israel invaded Gaza in October 2023 following the worst attack on the country in its history by Hamas, the toll on Palestinians and the wider issue of Palestinian rights have emerged as a rallying cry in the entertainment industry.
From the Oscars to the Emmys, top music awards ceremonies and European film festivals, the Gaza war has frequently pushed its way onto the agenda.

The massive Israeli offensive in Gaza has killed more than 73,800 people, according to the Gaza health ministry, which is under Hamas authority and whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.
On Saturday, Gaza authorities said the latest Israeli fire had killed at least four people, including a 10-year-old girl.
